## Other uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Other uses")]

### Sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Sports")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Atacamadunas.JPG/250px-Atacamadunas.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atacamadunas.JPG)

Patagonia-Atacama Rally in 2007

The Atacama Desert is popular with all-terrain sports enthusiasts. Various championships have taken place here, including the Lower Atacama Rally, Lower Chile Rally, Patagonia-Atacama Rally, and the latter [Dakar Rally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar_Rally "Dakar Rally")'s editions. The rally was organized by the [Amaury Sport Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_Sport_Organisation "Amaury Sport Organisation") and held in 2009, 2010, 2011, and 2012. The dunes of the desert are ideal rally races located in the outskirts of the city of Copiapó.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-80) The 2013 Dakar 15-Day Rally started on 5 January in Lima, Peru, through Chile, [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") and back to Chile finishing in Santiago.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-81) Visitors also use the Atacama Desert [sand dunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune "Dune") for [sandboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandboarding "Sandboarding") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _duna_).

A week-long foot race called the Atacama Crossing has the competitors cross the various landscapes of the Atacama.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-82)

An event called Volcano Marathon takes place near the [Lascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascar_(volcano) "Lascar (volcano)") volcano in the Atacama Desert.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-83)

### Solar car racing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Solar car racing")]

Eighteen [solar powered cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_car "Solar car") were displayed in front of the presidential palace (_La Moneda_) in Santiago in November 2012.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-84) The cars were then raced 1,300 km (810 mi) through the desert from 15 to 19 November 2012.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-85)

### Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Tourism")]

Most people who go to tour the sites in the desert stay in the town of San Pedro de Atacama.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-86) The Atacama Desert is in the top three tourist locations in Chile. The specially commissioned ESO hotel is reserved for astronomers and scientists.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-87)

### Storage battery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Storage battery")]

Since 2024 the Spanish company [Grenergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenergy "Grenergy") is building the "Oasis de Atacama" storage battery from photovoltaic energy. It has a capacity of about 2 GW solar together with 11 gigawatt hours (GWh) of storage.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-88)

Grenergy has an agreement with [BYD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYD_Company "BYD Company") for the supply of large-scale storage systems for a total capacity of 3GWh for Oasis de Atacama.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-89)

## El Tatio Geyser

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: El Tatio Geyser")]

Main article: [El Tatio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Tatio "El Tatio")

About 80 [geysers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geyser "Geyser") occur in a valley about 80 km from the town of San Pedro de Atacama, close to the town of Chiu Chiu.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-90)

## Termas Baños de Puritama

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Termas Baños de Puritama")]

The Baños de Puritama are rock pools which are 60 kilometres (37 miles) from the geysers.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-91)

The **Atacama Desert** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Desierto de Atacama_[[ataˈkama]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is a desert [plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau "Plateau") on the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") coast of [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America"), stretching along a 1,600-kilometre-long (1,000-mile) strip of land in northern [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile"), west of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes"). It covers an area of 105,000 km 2 (41,000 mi 2),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-nyt-2) rising to 128,000 km 2 (49,000 mi 2) if the barren lower slopes of the Andes are included.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-PGarid-3)

The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert in the world and the largest [fog desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_desert "Fog desert") on Earth.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-4) Extreme aridity results from its position between two mountain chains—the Andes and the [Chilean Coast Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_Coast_Range "Chilean Coast Range")—of sufficient height to block moisture from both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, creating a two-sided [rain shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-PhysGeogSA-5) The cool, north-flowing [Humboldt Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current "Humboldt Current") and the [South Pacific anticyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Pacific_High "South Pacific High") reinforce this effect.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-6) Average annual rainfall is around 15 mm (0.6 in) per year,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-ucmp-7) and some weather stations in the desert have never recorded rain. Evidence suggests the desert may have received no significant rainfall from 1570 to 1971,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-nyt-2) and hyper-arid conditions date back at least to the [Miocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miocene "Miocene").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-dx.doi.org-8)

The desert borders Peru to the north and the [Chilean Matorral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_Matorral "Chilean Matorral") ecoregion to the south, with the less arid [Central Andean dry puna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Andean_dry_puna "Central Andean dry puna") to the east. Its high altitude, dry air, and near-total absence of light pollution make it one of the world's premier sites for astronomical observation, hosting several major observatories including the [Atacama Large Millimeter Array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Large_Millimeter_Array "Atacama Large Millimeter Array") (ALMA) and the [Very Large Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very_Large_Telescope "Very Large Telescope").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Bustos-9) Its soil composition and near-total absence of microbial life have also made it a testing ground for [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") mission instruments.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Navarro-G_Marslike-10)

The desert has been inhabited since at least 7000 BCE, when the [Chinchorro culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinchorro_culture "Chinchorro culture") settled along its coast. Later peoples included the [Atacameño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_people "Atacama people") and, during the [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire"), Aymara communities. Under Spanish colonial rule, coastal towns developed as ports for silver exports; in the 19th century, rich deposits of [sodium nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_nitrate "Sodium nitrate") made the region a zone of conflict between Chile, Bolivia, and Peru, culminating in the [War of the Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Pacific "War of the Pacific").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-britannica.com-11) Today the desert is sparsely populated, with tourism, copper mining, and astronomical research as its principal industries.

## Setting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Setting")]

See also: [Andean orogeny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andean_orogeny "Andean orogeny") and [Arid Diagonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arid_Diagonal "Arid Diagonal")

According to the [World Wide Fund for Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Fund_for_Nature "World Wide Fund for Nature"), the Atacama Desert [ecoregion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecoregion "Ecoregion") occupies a continuous strip for nearly 1,600 kilometres (1,000 mi) along the narrow coast of the northern third of [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile"), from near [Arica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arica "Arica") (18°24′S) southward to near [La Serena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Serena,_Chile "La Serena, Chile") (29°55′S).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-12) The [National Geographic Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Society "National Geographic Society") considers the coastal area of southern [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") to be part of the Atacama Desert[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-NatGeo_Viking-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-NatGeo_GiantPenguin-14) and includes the deserts south of the [Ica Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Ica "Department of Ica") in Peru. However, other sources consider that the part of the desert in Peru is a different ecosystem, and should properly be named as Pampas de la Joya desert.

Peru borders it on the north and the [Chilean Matorral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_Matorral "Chilean Matorral") ecoregion borders it on the south. To the east lies the less arid [Central Andean dry Puna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Andean_dry_puna "Central Andean dry puna") ecoregion. [_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The drier portion of this ecoregion is located south of the [Loa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loa_River "Loa River") between the parallel [Sierra Vicuña Mackenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Vicu%C3%B1a_Mackenna "Sierra Vicuña Mackenna") and the [Cordillera Domeyko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Domeyko "Cordillera Domeyko").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] To the north of the Loa lies the [Pampa del Tamarugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampa_del_Tamarugal "Pampa del Tamarugal").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The [Coastal Cliff of northern Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_Cliff_of_northern_Chile "Coastal Cliff of northern Chile") west of the [Chilean Coast Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_Coast_Range "Chilean Coast Range") is the main topographical feature of the coast.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-15) The geomorphology of the Atacama Desert has been characterized as a low-relief bench "similar to a giant uplifted terrace" by Armijo and co-workers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Armijoetal2015-16) The intermediate depression (or Central Valley) forms a series of [endorheic basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorheic_basin "Endorheic basin") in much of the Atacama Desert south of latitude 19°30'S. North of this latitude, the intermediate depression drains into the Pacific Ocean.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Evenstaretal2014-17)

In December 2023, scientists, for the first time, reported on a recently discovered area in the territory of [Puna de Atacama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puna_de_Atacama "Puna de Atacama"), which may have similarities to Earth during the [Archean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archean "Archean") eon and thus to the environment of the [first life forms on Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earliest_known_life_forms "Earliest known life forms"). It could also be similar to conceivably-hospitable conditions on the planet [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") during earlier Martian times.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-CU-20231206-18)

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Climate")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Snow_Comes_to_the_Atacama_Desert.jpg/330px-Snow_Comes_to_the_Atacama_Desert.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Snow_Comes_to_the_Atacama_Desert.jpg)

Snow in [Paranal Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranal_Observatory "Paranal Observatory") at 2,600 [masl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M.a.s.l. "M.a.s.l.")[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-19)

The Atacama has a [cold desert climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_climate#Cold_desert_climates "Desert climate") (in the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), _BWk_) with generally mild temperatures year-round and only slight temperature differences across seasons. Rather than the intense heat of many other deserts around the world, the almost total lack of precipitation is the most prominent characteristic of the Atacama Desert.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-20)

### Aridity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Aridity")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Atacama_Desert_between_Antofagasta_and_Taltal.jpg/330px-Atacama_Desert_between_Antofagasta_and_Taltal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atacama_Desert_between_Antofagasta_and_Taltal.jpg)

A flat area of the Atacama Desert between Antofagasta and [Taltal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taltal "Taltal")

The Atacama Desert is commonly known as the driest place in the world, especially the surroundings of the abandoned Yungay mining town, where the [University of Antofagasta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Antofagasta "University of Antofagasta") Desert Research Station is located,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-21)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Navarro-G_Marslike-10) in [Antofagasta Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antofagasta_Region "Antofagasta Region"), Chile.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-TWP-22) The average rainfall is about 15 mm (0.6 in) per year,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-ucmp-7) although some locations receive only 1 to 3 mm (0.04 to 0.12 in) in a year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-nasa-23) Moreover, some weather stations in the Atacama have never received rain. Periods up to four years have been registered with no rainfall in the central sector, delimited by the cities of [Antofagasta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antofagasta "Antofagasta"), [Calama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calama,_Chile "Calama, Chile") and [Copiapó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copiap%C3%B3 "Copiapó").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-NatGeo_Driest-24) Evidence suggests that the Atacama may not have had any significant rainfall from 1570 to 1971.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-nyt-2)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Paisajes_cerca_de_Calama%2C_Chile%2C_2016-02-01%2C_DD_84_%28cropped%29.JPG/250px-Paisajes_cerca_de_Calama%2C_Chile%2C_2016-02-01%2C_DD_84_%28cropped%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paisajes_cerca_de_Calama,_Chile,_2016-02-01,_DD_84_(cropped).JPG)

Feral donkey in the Atacama desert

The Atacama Desert may be the oldest desert on earth, and has experienced hyper aridity since at least the [Middle Miocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Miocene "Middle Miocene"), since the establishment of a proto-Humboldt current in conjunction with the opening of the Tasmania-Antarctic passage ca. 33 million years ago ([Ma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megaannum "Megaannum")).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-dx.doi.org-8) The opening of the Tasmania-Antarctic passage allowed for cold currents to move along the west coast of South America, which influenced the availability of warm humid air to travel from the Amazon Basin to the Atacama. Though there was a general lack of humid air after 33 Ma, there were punctuated intervals of increased humidity,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-MedialdeaEtAl2020-25) such as between around 10.86 and 6.4 Ma, when the Tiliviche Palaeolake existed before turning into a [salar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_pan_(geology) "Salt pan (geology)") sometime before the Middle Pliocene.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Kirk-LawlorJordanRechLehmann2013-26) The long history of aridity raises the possibility that [supergene mineralisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergene_(geology) "Supergene (geology)"), under the appropriate conditions, can form in arid environments, instead of requiring humid conditions.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-ucmp2-27) The presence of [evaporite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaporite "Evaporite") formations suggests that in some sections of the Atacama Desert, arid conditions have persisted for the last 200 million years (since the [Triassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic "Triassic")).

Aridity in Atacama Desert predates the rise of the Central Andes, yet hyper-aridity is generally thought to have resulted from the rise of the Andes.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-namib-28) As such it is hypothesised it had climatic conditions akin to the [Namib Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namib "Namib") prior to the rise of the mountains.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-namib-28)

The Atacama is so arid that many mountains higher than 6,000 m (20,000 ft) are completely free of [glaciers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier "Glacier"). Only the highest peaks (such as [Ojos del Salado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojos_del_Salado "Ojos del Salado"), [Monte Pissis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Pissis "Monte Pissis"), and – [debatably](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llullaillaco#Snow_and_glaciers "Llullaillaco")[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchroderMakki20004-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERichardsVilleneuve200179-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEINdG201834%E2%80%9335-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEINdG201813-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVald%C3%A9s_Cantallops200220%E2%80%9321-33) – [Llullaillaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llullaillaco "Llullaillaco")) have some permanent snow coverage.

The southern part of the desert, between 25° and 27°S, may have been glacier-free throughout the [Quaternary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary "Quaternary") (including during [glaciations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_period "Glacial period")), though [permafrost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permafrost "Permafrost") extends down to an altitude of 4,400 m (14,400 ft) and is continuous above 5,600 m (18,400 ft). Studies by a group of British scientists have suggested that some river beds have been dry for 120,000 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-34) However, some locations in the Atacama receive a marine [fog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog "Fog") known locally as the _[camanchaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camanchaca "Camanchaca")_, providing sufficient moisture for hypolithic [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae"), [lichens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lichen "Lichen"), and even some [cacti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cactus "Cactus")—the genus _[Copiapoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copiapoa "Copiapoa")_ is notable among these.

Geographically, the aridity of the Atacama is explained by its being situated between two mountain chains (the Andes and the Chilean Coast Range) of sufficient height to prevent moisture [advection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advection "Advection") from either the Pacific or the Atlantic Oceans, a two-sided rain shadow.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-PhysGeogSA-5)

Despite modern views of the Atacama Desert as fully devoid of vegetation, in pre-Columbian and colonial times a large flatland area there known as [Pampa del Tamarugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampa_del_Tamarugal "Pampa del Tamarugal") was a [woodland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland "Woodland"), but demand for firewood associated with silver and [saltpeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitratine "Nitratine") mining in the 18th and 19th centuries resulted in widespread [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Castro2020-35)[[A]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-36)

### Comparison to Mars

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Comparison to Mars")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/A_trip_to_Mars.jpg/330px-A_trip_to_Mars.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_trip_to_Mars.jpg)

The lack of humidity, rain, and light pollution together produce a dusty, rocky landscape.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-37)

In a region about 100 km (60 mi) south of Antofagasta, which averages 3,000 m (10,000 ft) in elevation, the soil has been compared to that of [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"). Owing to its otherworldly appearance, the Atacama has been used as a location for filming Mars scenes, most notably in the 2004 television series _[Space Odyssey: Voyage to the Planets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Odyssey\_(TV\_series) "Space Odyssey (TV series)")_.

In 2003, a team of researchers published a report  in which they duplicated the tests used by the _[Viking 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking\_1 "Viking 1")_ and _[Viking 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking\_2 "Viking 2")_ Mars landers to detect life and were unable to detect any signs in Atacama Desert soil in the region of Yungay.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Navarro-G_Marslike-10) The region may be unique on Earth in this regard and is being used by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") to test instruments for future Mars missions. The team duplicated the Viking tests in Mars-like Earth environments and found that they missed present signs of life in soil samples from [Antarctic dry valleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMurdo_Dry_Valleys "McMurdo Dry Valleys"), the Atacama Desert of Chile and Peru, and other locales. However, in 2014, a new hyperarid site was reported, [María Elena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_Elena,_Chile "María Elena, Chile") South, which was much drier than Yungay and, thus, a better Mars-like environment.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Azua-Bustos_Discovery_and_microbial-38)

> Towards Atacama, near the deserted coast, you see a land without men, where there is not a bird, not a beast, nor a tree, nor any vegetation.

—_[La Araucana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Araucana "La Araucana")_ by [Alonso de Ercilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonso_de_Ercilla "Alonso de Ercilla"), 1569[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Braudel-39)

In 2008, the _[Phoenix Mars Lander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix\_(spacecraft) "Phoenix (spacecraft)")_ detected [perchlorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perchlorate "Perchlorate") on the surface of Mars at the same site where water was first discovered.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-40) Perchlorates are also found in the Atacama and associated nitrate deposits have contained organics, leading to speculation that signs of life on Mars are not incompatible with perchlorates. The Atacama is also a testing site for the NASA-funded _Earth–Mars Cave Detection Program_.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-41)

On 21 February 2023, scientists reported the findings of a "[dark microbiome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbial_dark_matter "Microbial dark matter")" of unfamiliar [microorganisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microorganism "Microorganism") in the Atacama Desert.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-WP-20230221-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-NC-20230221-43)

### Extreme weather events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Extreme weather events")]

In June 1991, [Antofagasta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antofagasta "Antofagasta") and [Taltal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taltal "Taltal") and inland regions as far as [Calama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calama,_Chile "Calama, Chile") received unusual rainfall leading to formation of [a series of mudflows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Antofagasta_mudflows "1991 Antofagasta mudflows") that killed 91 people.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-LaTercera2019-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-ElmerAn2007-46)

In 2012, the altiplano winter brought floods to [San Pedro de Atacama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Pedro_de_Atacama "San Pedro de Atacama").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-48)

On 25 March 2015, heavy rainfall affected the southern part of the Atacama Desert.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-lsc-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-blake-50) Resulting [floods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Northern_Chile_floods_and_mudflow "2015 Northern Chile floods and mudflow") triggered [mudflows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudflow "Mudflow") that affected the cities of [Copiapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copiap%C3%B3 "Copiapó"), [Tierra Amarilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tierra_Amarilla,_Chile "Tierra Amarilla, Chile"), [Chanaral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cha%C3%B1aral "Chañaral") and [Diego de Almagro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_de_Almagro,_Chile "Diego de Almagro, Chile"), causing the deaths of more than 100 people.

In early 2019, extreme heat and wildfires in Chile resulted in heavy flooding in the Atacama.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-51) At least 6 people died and 346 homes were destroyed.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-53)

## Flora

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Flora")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Desierto_florido.jpg/250px-Desierto_florido.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Desierto_florido.jpg)

Rare rainfall events cause the [flowering desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowering_desert_(Chile) "Flowering desert (Chile)") phenomenon in the southern Atacama Desert.

In spite of the geographic and climatic conditions of the desert, a rich variety of flora has evolved there. Over 500 species have been gathered within the border of this desert. These species are characterized by their extraordinary ability to adapt to this extreme environment.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-54) The most common species are herbs and flowers such as [thyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyme "Thyme"), [llareta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yareta "Yareta"), and [saltgrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distichlis_spicata "Distichlis spicata"), and where humidity is sufficient, trees such as the [tamarugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strombocarpa_tamarugo "Strombocarpa tamarugo") (endemic to the atacama), the [chañar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffroea_decorticans "Geoffroea decorticans"), the [pimiento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pimiento "Pimiento") tree and the leafy [algarrobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neltuma_chilensis "Neltuma chilensis").

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Pan_de_Azucar_National_Park.jpg/250px-Pan_de_Azucar_National_Park.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pan_de_Azucar_National_Park.jpg)

Vegetation in [Pan de Azúcar National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_de_Az%C3%BAcar_National_Park "Pan de Azúcar National Park") on the coast of the Atacama Desert

The llareta is one of the highest-growing wood species in the world. It is found at altitudes between 3,000 and 5,000 m (9,800 and 16,400 ft). Its dense form is similar to a pillow some 3 to 4 m (9.8 to 13.1 ft) thick. It concentrates and retains the heat from the day to cope with low evening temperatures. The growth rate of the llareta has been recently estimated at 1.5 cm/year (0.59 in/year), making many llaretas over 3,000 years old. It produces a much-prized resin, which the mining industry once harvested indiscriminately as fuel, making this plant endangered.

The desert is also home to cacti, succulents, and other plants that thrive in a dry climate. Cactus species here include the [candelabro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browningia_candelaris "Browningia candelaris") and [cardon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leucostele_atacamensis "Leucostele atacamensis"), which can reach a height of 7 m (23 ft) and a diameter of 70 cm (28 in).

The Atacama Desert [flowering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_bloom "Desert bloom") (_[Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish\_language "Spanish language"): \_desierto florido\__) can be seen from September to November in years with sufficient precipitation, as happened in 2015.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-lsc-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-blake-50)

## Fauna

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Fauna")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Atacama_Desert.jpg/250px-Atacama_Desert.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atacama_Desert.jpg)

[Andean flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andean_flamingo "Andean flamingo") in Salar de Atacama

The climate of the Atacama Desert limits the number of animals living permanently in this extreme ecosystem. Some parts of the desert are so [arid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aridity "Aridity"), no plant or animal life can survive. Outside of these extreme areas, sand-colored [grasshoppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grasshopper "Grasshopper") blend with pebbles on the desert floor, and [beetles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beetle "Beetle") and their [larvae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larva "Larva") provide a valuable food source in the _[lomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lomas "Lomas")_ (hills). Desert [wasps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasp "Wasp") and [butterflies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butterfly "Butterfly") can be found during the warm and humid season, especially on the lomas. Red [scorpions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorpion "Scorpion") also live in the desert.

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Atacama_lizard1.jpg/250px-Atacama_lizard1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atacama_lizard1.jpg)

_[Liolaemus nitidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liolaemus\_nitidus "Liolaemus nitidus")_, a lizard native to the southern reaches of the Atacama Desert

A unique environment is provided by some _lomas_, where the fog from the ocean provides enough moisture for seasonal plants and a few animal species. Surprisingly few [reptile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile "Reptile") species inhabit the desert and even fewer [amphibian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibian "Amphibian") species. The [Vallenar toad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhinella_atacamensis "Rhinella atacamensis") (also called the Atacama toad), lives on the _lomas_, where it lays eggs in permanent ponds or streams. [Iguanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguana "Iguana") and [lava lizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microlophus "Microlophus") inhabit parts of the desert, while [salt flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_pan_(geology) "Salt pan (geology)") lizards, _[Liolaemus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liolaemus "Liolaemus")_, live in the dry areas bordering the ocean.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-55) One species, _[Liolaemus fabiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liolaemus\_fabiani "Liolaemus fabiani")_, is endemic to the [Salar de Atacama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Atacama "Salar de Atacama"), the Atacama salt flat.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-56)

Birds are one of the most diverse animal groups in the Atacama. [Humboldt penguins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_penguin "Humboldt penguin") live year-round along the coast, nesting in desert cliffs overlooking the ocean. Inland, high-altitude salt flats are inhabited by [Andean flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andean_flamingo "Andean flamingo"), while [Chilean flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_flamingo "Chilean flamingo") can be seen along the coast. Other birds (including species of [hummingbirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hummingbird "Hummingbird") and [rufous-collared sparrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rufous-collared_sparrow "Rufous-collared sparrow")) visit the _lomas_ seasonally to feed on insects, nectar, seeds, and flowers. The _lomas_ help sustain several threatened species, such as the endangered [Chilean woodstar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_woodstar "Chilean woodstar").

Because of the desert's extreme aridity, only a few specially adapted mammal species live in the Atacama, such as [Darwin's leaf-eared mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwin's_leaf-eared_mouse "Darwin's leaf-eared mouse"). The less arid parts of the desert are inhabited by the [South American gray fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_American_gray_fox "South American gray fox") and the [viscacha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscacha "Viscacha") (a relative of the [chinchilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinchilla "Chinchilla")). Larger animals, such as [guanacos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanaco "Guanaco") and [vicuñas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicu%C3%B1a "Vicuña"), graze in areas where grass grows, mainly because it is seasonally irrigated by melted snow. Vicuñas need to remain near a steady water supply, while guanacos can roam into more arid areas and survive longer without fresh water. [South American fur seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_American_fur_seal "South American fur seal") and [South American sea lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_American_sea_lion "South American sea lion") often gather along the coast.

The Atacama is sparsely populated, with most towns located along the Pacific coast.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-57) In interior areas, oases and some valleys have been populated for millennia and were the location of the most advanced pre-Columbian societies found in Chile.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Chinchorro culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Chinchorro culture")]

Main article: [Chinchorro culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinchorro_culture "Chinchorro culture")

The Chinchorro culture developed in the Atacama Desert area from 7000 BCE to 1500 BCE. These peoples were sedentary fishermen inhabiting mostly coastal areas. Their presence is found from today's towns of [Ilo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilo_province "Ilo province"), in southern Peru, to [Antofagasta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antofagasta "Antofagasta") in northern Chile. Presence of fresh water in the arid region on the coast facilitated human settlement in these areas. The Chinchorro were famous for their detailed [mummification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mummy "Mummy") and funerary practices.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-58)

### Inca and Spanish empires

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Inca and Spanish empires")]

[San Pedro de Atacama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Pedro_de_Atacama "San Pedro de Atacama"), at about 2,400 m (8,000 ft) elevation, is like many of the small towns. Before the [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire") and prior to the arrival of the Spanish, the extremely arid interior was inhabited primarily by the [Atacameño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_people "Atacama people") tribe. They are noted for building fortified towns called _[pucarás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pukara\_culture "Pukara culture")_, one of which is located a few kilometers from San Pedro de Atacama. The town's church was built by the [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") in 1577.

The Atacameño[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-59) were an extinct Indigenous South American culture,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-60) different from the [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_people "Aymara people") to the north and the [Diaguita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diaguita "Diaguita") to the south.

The oasis settlement of [Pica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pica,_Chile "Pica, Chile") has Pre-Hispanic origins and served as an important stopover for transit between the coast and the [Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano "Altiplano") during the time of the [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-61)

During the Inca Empire [Moyos Moyos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moyos_Moyos "Moyos Moyos"), whose tentative homeland lies in [Tarija Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Valley_of_Tarija?action=edit&redlink=1 "Central Valley of Tarija (page does not exist)"), were settled in the desert as part of a [population transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitma "Mitma") scheme.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-barcon-62)

The coastal cities originated in the 16th, 17th, and 18th centuries during the time of the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"), when they emerged as shipping ports for [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver") produced in [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí") and other mining centers. At the end of the 18th century, Carlos IV defines the southern border of the Viceroyalty of Peru at the port of Nuestra Señora del Paposo.

### Republican period

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Republican period")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Pampa_del_Tamarugal_2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Pampa_del_Tamarugal_2_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pampa_del_Tamarugal_2_(cropped).jpg)

View of a forest in [Pampa del Tamarugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampa_del_Tamarugal "Pampa del Tamarugal") from [Chile Route 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile_Route_5 "Chile Route 5"). These forests were once devastated by the demand of firewood associated with saltpeter mining.

During the 19th century, the desert came under control of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), Chile and Peru. With the discovery of [sodium nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_nitrate "Sodium nitrate") deposits and as a result of Chilean expansion plans, the area soon became a zone of conflict and resulted in the [War of the Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Pacific "War of the Pacific"). Chile annexed most of the desert, and cities along the coast developed into international ports, hosting many Chilean workers who migrated there.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-63)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-65)

With the guano and saltpeter booms of the 19th century, the population grew immensely, mostly as a result of immigration from central Chile. In the 20th century, the nitrate industry declined and at the same time, the largely male population of the desert became increasingly problematic for the Chilean state. Miners and mining companies came into conflict, and protests spread throughout the region.

Around 1900, there were irrigation system of [puquios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puquios "Puquios") spread through the oases of Atacama Desert.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Licteetal2020-66) Puquios are known from the valleys of [Azapa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azapa_Valley "Azapa Valley") and [Sibaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibaya "Sibaya") and the oases of [La Calera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Calera_(oasis) "La Calera (oasis)"), [Pica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pica,_Chile "Pica, Chile")-[Matilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matilla "Matilla") and [Puquio de Núñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puquio_de_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez "Puquio de Núñez").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Licteetal2020-66) In 1918, geologist [Juan Brüggen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Br%C3%BCggen "Juan Brüggen") mentioned the existence of 23 _socavones_ (shafts) in the Pica oasis, yet these have since been abandoned due to economic and social changes.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Licteetal2020-66)

### Abandoned nitrate mining towns

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Abandoned nitrate mining towns")]

Main article: [List of saltpeter works in Tarapacá and Antofagasta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_saltpeter_works_in_Tarapac%C3%A1_and_Antofagasta "List of saltpeter works in Tarapacá and Antofagasta")

The desert has rich deposits of [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper") and other [minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral "Mineral") and the world's largest natural supply of [sodium nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_nitrate "Sodium nitrate"), which was mined on a large scale until the early 1940s. The [Atacama border dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert_border_dispute "Atacama Desert border dispute") over these resources between Chile and Bolivia began in the 19th century and resulted in the [War of the Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Pacific "War of the Pacific").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-britannica.com-11)

The desert is littered with about 170 abandoned nitrate mining towns, almost all of which were shut down following the invention of synthetic nitrate in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") in the first decade of the 20th century (see [Haber process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haber_process "Haber process")).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The towns include [Chacabuco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chacabuco "Chacabuco"), [Humberstone, Santa Laura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humberstone_and_Santa_Laura_Saltpeter_Works "Humberstone and Santa Laura Saltpeter Works"), Pedro de Valdivia, Puelma, [María Elena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_Elena,_Chile "María Elena, Chile"), and Oficina Anita.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Atacama Desert is rich in metallic mineral resources such as copper, gold, silver and iron, as well as nonmetallic minerals including important deposits of boron, lithium, sodium nitrate, and potassium salts. The Salar de Atacama is where [bischofite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bischofite "Bischofite") is extracted.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The Atacama Desert is also the world's largest source of [iodine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodine "Iodine")-bearing minerals, with some areas having iodine concentrations hundreds of times larger than the average levels in Earth's crust.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-67) These resources are exploited by various mining companies such as Codelco, Lomas Bayas, Mantos Blancos, and Soquimich.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-69)

### Pollution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Pollution")]

In recent years, large amounts of used clothing imported from overseas have begun to accumulate in portions of the desert. The desert is estimated to receive around 39,000 tonnes of illegally dumped used clothing each year, according to the highest available estimates.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-70) Because of the dry conditions, they do not decompose at the normal rate, and fires have exposed nearby residents to air pollution.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-71)

## Astronomical observatories

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Astronomical observatories")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/ALMA_and_the_centre_of_the_Milky_Way.jpg/250px-ALMA_and_the_centre_of_the_Milky_Way.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ALMA_and_the_centre_of_the_Milky_Way.jpg)

[ALMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Large_Millimeter_Array "Atacama Large Millimeter Array") and the center of the [Milky Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milky_Way "Milky Way")[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-72)

Because of its high altitude, nearly nonexistent cloud cover, dry air, and freedom from light pollution and radio interference from widely populated cities and towns, this desert is one of the best places in the world to conduct astronomical observations.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-73)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-Bustos-9) Hundreds of thousands of stars can be viewed via telescope since the desert experiences more than 200 cloudless nights each year. A number of telescopes have been installed to help [astronomers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomer "Astronomer") from across the globe study the universe.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-74) A [radio astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_astronomy "Radio astronomy") telescope, called the [Atacama Large Millimeter Array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Large_Millimeter_Array "Atacama Large Millimeter Array"), built by [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") countries, [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), and [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile") in the [Llano de Chajnantor Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llano_de_Chajnantor_Observatory "Llano de Chajnantor Observatory") officially opened on 3 October 2011.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-75) A number of radio astronomy projects, such as the [CBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_Background_Imager "Cosmic Background Imager"), the [ASTE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Submillimeter_Telescope_Experiment "Atacama Submillimeter Telescope Experiment") and the [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Cosmology_Telescope "Atacama Cosmology Telescope"), among others, have been operating in the Chajnantor area since 1999. On 26 April 2010, the [ESO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Southern_Observatory "European Southern Observatory") council decided to build a fourth site, [Cerro Armazones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Armazones "Cerro Armazones"), to be home to the [Extremely Large Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremely_Large_Telescope "Extremely Large Telescope").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-76)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-78) Construction work at the ELT site started in June 2014.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-beginning-79) The [Carnegie Institution for Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Institution_for_Science "Carnegie Institution for Science") operates the [Las Campanas Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Campanas_Observatory "Las Campanas Observatory") with several telescopes in the southern portion of the desert.

The [European Southern Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Southern_Observatory "European Southern Observatory") operates three major [observatories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observatory "Observatory") in the Atacama and is currently building a fourth:

*   [La Silla Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Silla_Observatory "La Silla Observatory")
*   [Paranal Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranal_Observatory "Paranal Observatory"), which includes the [Very Large Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very_Large_Telescope "Very Large Telescope") (VLT)
*   [Llano de Chajnantor Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llano_de_Chajnantor_Observatory "Llano de Chajnantor Observatory"), which hosts the [ALMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Large_Millimeter_Array "Atacama Large Millimeter Array") international radio observatory
*   [Cerro Armazones Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Armazones_Observatory "Cerro Armazones Observatory"), site of the future [Extremely Large Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremely_Large_Telescope "Extremely Large Telescope") (ELT)

## Other uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Other uses")]

### Sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Sports")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Atacamadunas.JPG/250px-Atacamadunas.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atacamadunas.JPG)

Patagonia-Atacama Rally in 2007

The Atacama Desert is popular with all-terrain sports enthusiasts. Various championships have taken place here, including the Lower Atacama Rally, Lower Chile Rally, Patagonia-Atacama Rally, and the latter [Dakar Rally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar_Rally "Dakar Rally")'s editions. The rally was organized by the [Amaury Sport Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_Sport_Organisation "Amaury Sport Organisation") and held in 2009, 2010, 2011, and 2012. The dunes of the desert are ideal rally races located in the outskirts of the city of Copiapó.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-80) The 2013 Dakar 15-Day Rally started on 5 January in Lima, Peru, through Chile, [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") and back to Chile finishing in Santiago.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-81) Visitors also use the Atacama Desert [sand dunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune "Dune") for [sandboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandboarding "Sandboarding") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _duna_).

A week-long foot race called the Atacama Crossing has the competitors cross the various landscapes of the Atacama.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-82)

An event called Volcano Marathon takes place near the [Lascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascar_(volcano) "Lascar (volcano)") volcano in the Atacama Desert.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-83)

### Solar car racing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Solar car racing")]

Eighteen [solar powered cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_car "Solar car") were displayed in front of the presidential palace (_La Moneda_) in Santiago in November 2012.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-84) The cars were then raced 1,300 km (810 mi) through the desert from 15 to 19 November 2012.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-85)

### Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Tourism")]

Most people who go to tour the sites in the desert stay in the town of San Pedro de Atacama.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-86) The Atacama Desert is in the top three tourist locations in Chile. The specially commissioned ESO hotel is reserved for astronomers and scientists.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-87)

### Storage battery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atacama_Desert&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Storage battery")]

Since 2024 the Spanish company [Grenergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenergy "Grenergy") is building the "Oasis de Atacama" storage battery from photovoltaic energy. It has a capacity of about 2 GW solar together with 11 gigawatt hours (GWh) of storage.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-88)

Grenergy has an agreement with [BYD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYD_Company "BYD Company") for the supply of large-scale storage systems for a total capacity of 3GWh for Oasis de Atacama.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-89)

About 80 [geysers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geyser "Geyser") occur in a valley about 80 km from the town of San Pedro de Atacama, close to the town of Chiu Chiu.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert#cite_note-90)

## Abstract

The ecological value of coastal wetlands is globally recognized, particularly as biodiversity hotspots, but also as buffer areas because of their role in the fight against climate change in recent years. Most of Chile’s coastal wetlands are concentrated in the central and southern part of the country due to climate conditions. However, northern coastal wetlands go unnoticed despite being located in areas of high water deficit (desert areas) and their role in bird migratory routes along the north–south coastal cordon of South America. This study reviews the current environmental status of the arid coastal wetlands of northern Chile (Lluta, Camarones, Loa, La Chimba, Copiapó, Totoral, Carrizal Bajo) in terms of regulations, management, and future aims. The main natural and anthropogenic threats to these coastal wetlands are identified, as well as the main management tools applied for their protection, e.g., the Nature Sanctuary designation, which allows for the protection of both privately and publicly owned property; and the Urban Wetland, a recently created protection category.

Keywords:

[coastal wetlands](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=coastal+wetlands); [Atacama Desert](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=Atacama+Desert); [management tools](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=management+tools); [Ramsar](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=Ramsar); [nature sanctuary](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=nature+sanctuary)

## 1. Introduction

Coastal wetlands are aquatic ecosystems that sustain rich biodiversity and provide important ecosystem services, as defined by the Convention on Wetlands (Ramsar, Iran, 1971 [1]). They are areas of high ecological value, where terrestrial and marine environments converge, sharing various characteristics and threats to which they are exposed [2]. In Chile, with almost 6500 km of coastline, the distribution of coastal wetlands decreases in latitude from south to north, where they emerge scattered along the coastal area, forming a valuable corridor with high biodiversity, productivity, and endemism. They bear considerable relevance for ecosystem services, providing the coastal population with fisheries habitats, carbon sequestration, water filtration, and sediment trapping [3,4]. Moreover, they are essential as refuges for a wide variety of species of flora and migratory birds that migrate along the “Pacific-West”, “Central”, and “Patagonia” flyways [4], meaning its connectivity is indispensable.

These coastal wetlands are exposed to a wide range of threats of both natural and anthropogenic origin that have a potential dramatic impact upon their biodiversity and geomorphological configuration [5]. These cause northern Chile coastal wetlands to be in a critical condition in terms of vulnerability, resilience, and sustainability, aggravated by the current global changes [6]. Consequently, it is vital and urgent to devise distinct environmental protection categories ensuring the conservation and preservation of these systems of high ecological value [7]. Coastal wetlands develop in very dissimilar physiographic, hydro(geo)logical, and climatic contexts, giving them very heterogeneous features that generate varying degrees of vulnerability, resilience, or differential responses to threats. Thus, in territories marked by profound transformations in their geography, climate, and degree of anthropic occupation, as is the case in Chile, there are unanticipated differences among the coastal wetlands. This creates different scenarios of vulnerability that may not be contemplated, or sufficiently nuanced, by the environmental protection regulations, creating situations in which the safeguarding of these natural systems and, finally, their conservation are not guaranteed.

Arid coastal wetlands have been mainly studied for their ecological, edaphic, and hydrogeological features [8,9,10], whereas studies focused on their management and conservation are more scarce compared with those of temperate and tropic wetlands. The reason behind this difference is that they represent complex hydrogeological systems in which small changes in their hydrological regime can cause modifications in the groundwater chemistry, in the development of the soil profile, in the vegetation, etc. [11,12]. In fact, even though the ever-increasing water demands of industry and agriculture, coupled with the sensitivity of the wetlands to the irregular hydrographic conditions characteristic of arid and semiarid zones, renders them particularly vulnerable, they have received little attention in recent scientific literature (e.g., [13,14]).

In northern Chile, these coastal systems have a very precarious equilibrium, dependent on the maintenance of freshwater flows from river basins. At present, those river basins are subject to interventions by human activity, primarily caused by the overexploitation of aquifers by agricultural and mining activity. Furthermore, these arid coastal wetlands are severely threatened by a wide variety of both natural (winter storms, tsunamis, sea-level rise, and droughts) and anthropogenic processes (urban sewage, industrial waste, the advancement of agricultural and urban borders, the effect of introduced species and irrigation ditches, clandestine landfills, and the lack of legal and practical mechanisms ensuring the future viability of the few currently protected wetlands). These both seriously jeopardize their conservation in the coming decades [4,15]. As a result, the wetlands located in one of the most arid areas of the world, the Atacama Desert, may well be considered ecosystems in a fragile condition.

Because of the sparse distribution of coastal wetlands in northern Chile and their crucial ecological relevance, this study aims to highlight their meaning and significance despite having been poorly studied from a holistic perspective. In fact, so far, the analysis of their ecological, geomorphological, and hydro(geo)logical features, integrated with the threats they are exposed to, their environmental degradation, their heritage value and their legal protection, has not been previously carried out. Therefore, the main objectives of this work are (i) to review their recent environmental history; (ii) to catalogue and assess the different threats to which they are exposed; and (iii) to evaluate whether the Chilean environmental legislation has considered the particularities of these ecosystems and its adequacy and sufficiency to ensure their continuity in the short and long term. These coastal-marine spaces are valuable not only environmentally, but also socio-culturally. They have been strongly connected with the history of the occupation and use of the territory by humans for thousands of years until the last decades, when the recent population growth and the anthropogenic pressure has put coastal wetlands of northern Chile at risk [16].

## 2. Materials and Methods

A review of the available literature was made in terms of vulnerability factors, threats, legal framework, and coastal management tools applied to northern Chile coastal wetlands. The main instrument for information analysis was the National Inventory of Wetlands 2020 [17] that georeferenced all of the wetlands of Chile. The database was used for the identification of the wetlands, determining their location, characteristics, and distances, along with other international databases, such as the Ramsar site list. The legal framework consultancy was obtained through the National Congress Library (BCN). Moreover, the gray literature contained in the different ministries was also reviewed. In most cases, these unpublished government reports were the only available information source, in addition to undergraduate or graduate theses from local universities. For the scientific literature review, we used the customary academic databases.

## 3. Coastal Zone Management: Legal and Institutional Framework

The state of Chile shows a centralizing tendency that has dominated national decisions since individual regions have historically had a relatively minor role in decision-making [18]. Likewise, administrative organizations range from those at a national scale, managing the coast and its resources, and those at a local scale, responsible for planning and managing land use [19]. The result is that policymaking is distributed among a vast number of institutions of which the territorial planning regulations are designed to regulate urban territory more efficiently than non-urban territory, generating differences in the effectiveness of regulation, being particularly noticeable on the coast [20].

The administration of the coastal edge corresponds to the Ministry of National Defense, which exercises the control, inspection, and supervision of the coast and territorial sea of Chile (Figure 1, Table S1). It has the ability to grant concessions for the use of the coastal zone, making it one of the most relevant institutions in the organization of the coastal edge [18]. In 1994, the National Policy on Coastal Edge Use (PNUBC) was approved, representing the first step towards coastal zone management. The coastal edge was defined as the territorial zone that includes land and sea extending from the highest tidal line 80 m towards the land and 12 miles towards the sea. It includes beach lands, beaches, bays, gulfs, straits, inland channels, and the entire territorial sea of Chile [18]. The essential planning instruments of the PNUBC are constituted by the National Commission on Coastal Edge Use (CNUBC), comprising representatives of several ministries and governmental agencies with competence in the coastal edge [21], the function of which is to define coastal zoning [22]. The CNUBC established that the fourteen coastal regions of Chile should carry out its coastal zoning by means of the Regional Commissions on Coastal Edge Use (CRUBC). In 2018, competences were granted to the Regional Governments (GORE) regarding land-use planning through a new territorial planning instrument, the Regional Territorial Ordering Plan (PROT) [5], which defines the preferential uses of the coast at a regional level. Other government agencies also have competences in the administration of the coastal edge. The General Directorate of the Territory and the Merchant Marine (DIRECTEMAR) is responsible for complying with the laws and international agreements in force in the maritime area of its jurisdiction. Similarly, the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Service (SERNAPESCA) oversees compliance with fisheries and aquaculture regulations and exercises the supervision of Marine Parks and Reserves (Figure 1).

When authority over protected areas in coastal zones are considered, the number of institutions involved increases (Figure 1, Table S1). The National Forestry Corporation (CONAF) administers the National System of Protected Wild Areas of the State (SNASPE), with a specific program for the conservation of wetlands (National Program for the Conservation of Wetlands within SNASPE [23]), in which the northern coastal wetlands were not included. The Ministry of the Environment (MMA) manages the Multipurpose Coastal Marine Protected Area (CMAPMU), guards the Nature Sanctuaries (SNs) and supervises the entire system of protected areas.

Chile has acquired some international compromises that have promoted several national and regional regulations to protect the coastal wetlands (Table S1). The Ramsar Convention (1971) has been acknowledged by the Chilean Government since 1981 through Decree 771 of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Chile currently hosts sixteen sites designated as Wetlands of International Importance (Ramsar sites), which implies a surface area of 363,927 hectares. Although Ramsar sites are highly variable, coastal wetlands have gained greater relevance in recent years due to their ecological, geological, and chemical role in the fight against climate change; and the consequences of other natural events occurring in Chile (e.g., tsunamis, flood mitigation, droughts, etc.). The last designated Wetlands of International Importance have been coastal wetlands: Tongoy Bay (Coquimbo, 2018), Monkul wetland (Araucanía, 2020), and Limari River, from Salala to its mouth (Coquimbo, 2020). There are only eight designated Ramsar sites classified as marine or coastal wetlands in Chile, equalling 69,315 ha [24]. However, none of them is located in northern Chile. Hence, it is imperative to pinpoint that the absence of protection categories, such as Ramsar sites, exposes these areas to fragmentation and puts at risk coastal migration routes (i.e., threats for bird nesting and migration).

The MMA manages the National Plan for Wetland Protection 2018–2022 [25] (Table S1), which aims to stop the detriment of wetlands and to preserve biodiversity (protection of 40 wetlands/250,351 ha, including some coastal wetlands). Each wetland will be associated with a protected area category (Figure 2) and will be accompanied by regulations and institutions responsible for its protection [25]. In Chile, there are nine official protected-area categories that meet the following criteria: (i) biodiversity conservation; (ii) have management plans and; (iii) have institutional mechanisms for their planning, designation, and management [26] (Figure 2). In conjunction with these official categories, there are other conservation instruments such as international protection categories or other protective categories that are not protected areas. Some examples include buffer zones, conservation landscapes, biological corridors, and priority sites for biodiversity conservation (Figure 2). Recently, several northern coastal wetlands have been included in the National Plan for Wetland Protection 2018–2022. The main category used is Nature Sanctuary (Law 17.288 [27]), which is the only category that allows for the protection of both privately and publicly owned property, making it a flexible model. The Ministry of Cultures has the authority to declare the areas that are protected under this category, as well as the power to authorize the projects and/or activities that are carried out in them; yet it does not have the competence to administrate these areas. They are under the custody of the MMA. Nature Sanctuaries are considered in the same way as any terrestrial or marine sites with distinct possibilities for geological, paleontological, zoological, botanical or ecological studies, and research; or containing natural formations that should be reserved for scientific or governmental interest. The category of Nature Sanctuary for wetlands requires, among other things, “that all work execution, programs or activities to be developed inside and that are likely to cause environmental impact must be submitted to the Environmental Impact Assessment System (SEIA). In other words, projects require permits that ensure the object conservation of the protected areas” [28].

In 2020, the sustainability of the urban wetlands was considered under Law 21.202 [29] (Table S1), whereby the Ministry of Public Works (MOP) and the MMA will establish the minimum criteria to preserve their ecological characteristics and functioning, and the maintenance of the hydrological regime, both surface and underground. This law provides municipalities with concrete tools that will allow the protection of urban wetlands, by the drafting of General Ordinances for the protection of urban wetlands and the postponement of permits for property subdivision, urbanization, and construction.

## 4. The Arid Coastal Wetlands of Northern Chile

In this study, we focused on seven coastal wetlands of northern Chile: the Lluta (LLU) and Camarones (CAM) rivers’ mouths in the Arica and Parinacota Region; the Loa (LOA) river mouth and La Chimba (CHI) in the Antofagasta Region; and the Copiapó (COP) river mouth, Totoral (TOT); and Carrizal Bajo (CAR) in the Atacama Region (Figure 3). The extreme aridity of these regions, with a De Martonne aridity index (IDM) [30] lower than 0.5, makes them highly sensitive to natural or anthropogenic changes. Thus, a review of their threats and their legal protection status is key, and urgent to guarantee their future. Other arid wetlands located in the southern Atacama Desert coast with higher IDMs (e.g., the Huasco wetland with IDM ~1.45) or without an abundant supply of surface or groundwater (e.g., Mejillones Bay) have not been considered in this work. Finally, after the 2015 extreme hydrometeorological event, the Salado River eroded the beach located at its mouth and two new lagoons were formed that are currently being vegetated [31,32]. This newly formed wetland was not included either, awaiting its evolution in the dynamic littoral system.

The studied coastal wetlands are distributed along more than 1000 km of coastline, covering four Chilean territorial macrounits (regions), all of them located on the Atacama Desert coast from 18° S to 28° S (Figure 3). This coastline is classified as mixed semidiurnal and microtidal, with a mean tidal range of ~0.9 m. The dominant swell direction is SW, with significant wave heights of 1.79–2.04 m [33]. Specifically, data collected on the coast of the Chilean Atacama Desert by Campos et al. [34] indicate that the average and most frequent source of storm swell is from the southwest, accompanied by noticeable average wave heights close to 3 m, with maximum values of 5 m, that is, considerably lower values than the rest of the Chilean coastline. However, the analysis of the storm significant height extreme values projections shows a considerable significative increase in this parameter for the coming decades [35].

From a geodynamic perspective, the subduction margin of the Nazca plate beneath the South American plate along northern Chile is considered among the major seismic gaps worldwide. Convergence along this large tectonic margin occurs in a northeastern direction at a rate of ~65–67 mm/yr [36] and may be regarded as a highly coupled interplate subduction contact [37]. Along this major seismic gap, great numbers of tsunamigenic earthquakes of moderate magnitude (Mw 7–8.5) have occurred in the last centuries (the most recent the 2014 CE Mw~8.2 event). The major and most highly destructive events were the 1420 CE Mw~9, the 1868 CE Mw~8.6–8.8, the 1877 CE Mw~−8.8–8.9, and the 1922 CE Mw~8.6 events, with associated run-ups between 8–20 m a.s.l. These extensive interpolate seismic events produce substantial ecosystemic and geomorphologic damages [38,39,40,41], as well as considerable tectonic uplift (>1 m) of some coastal segments, which may consequently drastically affect coastal wetlands [42,43].

The geomorphology of the coastal area of the Atacama Desert is characterized by the presence of various Pleistocene marine terrace levels with heights between the current sea-level and 250 m a.s.l. (e.g., [44,45]). These terraces develop in the western foothills of the Andes Range, defined here by the Coastal Range, formed by Palaeozoic metamorphic rocks and Mesozoic sedimentary rocks intruded by plutonic igneous rocks. The Coastal Range constitutes an orientated N-S relief with variable widths of 10 to 25 km, which is intermittently cut by ravines of episodic and torrential behavior, as well as small rivers that reach the coastline. These latter features define very incised and narrow river valleys, where the occurrence of wetlands is possible.

The study area is an intertropical arid area that belongs to the biogeographical province of the Coastal Desert, dominated by the influence of the southeast Pacific subtropical anticyclone and modulated by the El Niño southern oscillation (ENSO), with a two- to seven-year periodicity, and the Pacific decadal oscillation (PDO), with 20- to 30-year periods [46,47]. The Atacama Desert’s extremely arid conditions are controlled by the presence of the Coastal and Andean Ranges [48], the cold oceanic waters of the Humboldt current system [49,50], and the southerly wind-driven coastal upwelling events occurring throughout the year [49,51]. Rainfall in the study area tends to increase with latitude [52] with mean annual values that range from 1.5 mm in Arica (18.4° S) to 35.9 mm in Huasco (28.1° S), south of the study area [53] (Figure 3). Despite coastal fog, a distinguishable feature of the local climate that provides water to a hyperarid environment and isolated ecosystems (e.g., [54,55,56,57]), the area is classified as hyperarid as the IDM is <0.5 [30]. Thus, desertic landscapes with coastal xerophilic scrub dominate as vegetation is scarce except along the transverse (east–west) valleys of the rivers that flow from the Andes range to the Pacific Ocean, crossing the desert and fed at high altitudes [4]. Along this coastline of arid northern Chile, small wetlands appear scattered around the mouths of river valleys and streams, fed by small springs or surface waters of very limited flows. Therefore, the presence of the coastal wetlands acquires a special importance as a connective network, drought combat, geophysical barrier, and the host of a huge number of endemic species [58].

The studied coastal wetlands have a total area of 1962 ha (Figure 4). In general, their area does not become larger toward less arid conditions, i.e., higher latitudes, since their formation and surface area are mainly controlled by surface and groundwater supply. This factor is then conditioned by the physiography, the hydrogeology, and the features of the watersheds, including human intervention in the upper sectors of the basins. Hence, the most important wetlands are those with higher watershed extensions—the Lluta, Camarones, and Copiapó wetlands, which represent a sharp increase in the accumulated area, shown in Figure 4. The other coastal wetlands, generally with areas below 50 ha, correspond to systems located at the mouths of episodic ravine or springs. In the case of the Loa River, even though it is one of the longest rivers in Chile, the groundwater extraction and the intervention of its channel over the last decades has led to the occurrence of a coastal wetland with a very limited area of only 30 ha [15].

### 4.1. Lluta River Wetland

The Lluta river is an exoreic river that exhibits its most important floods due to the highland winter rains [15]. It has a length of 147 km and covers an area of 3378 km 2 (Figure 5A). It has scarce vegetation in the upper part of the basin that increases in the lower parts. Its medium discharge rate in the river mouth is 1.4 m 3/s, with quantified minimum values of 0.09 m 3/s, whereas the medium flow rate entry is 2.5 m 3/s [59]. On the other hand, during very rainy years, especially those associated with ENSO events, its conditions may vary violently, with outflows of up to 4.5 m 3/s.
